summary: MPLS LSP Ping and Traceroute use a Reply Mode field to say how the echo reply should travel. This standards-track RFC changes the procedure for the Reply via Specified Path mode, value 5, giving a simpler way to say which return path to use. It updates RFC 7110.

eli5.summary: When you ask someone to write back, you can say which road the answer should take. This makes it simpler to name that road.

questions: what is lsp ping reply mode 5
what is the reply mode order tlv
what is a false failure in lsp ping
subtitle: A simpler way to tell an LSP Ping responder how to reply, plus a ranked list of fallback return paths.

tldr.problem: Choosing a return path that really works for an MPLS echo reply is hard, and a wrong guess makes the reply vanish and the test report a false failure.
tldr.mechanism: The 'Reply via Specified Path' Reply Mode (value 5) may now be used without a Reply Path TLV to mean the reverse LSP, and a new optional Reply Mode Order TLV lists several Reply Modes in preferred order.
tldr.outcome: The responder uses the first return path it has available, so fewer replies are lost. It updates RFC 7110 and is a Standards Track document.

today: RFC 7737 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2016. It updates RFC 7110 and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
MPLS LSP Ping (RFC 4379) lets an initiator Label Switching Router (LSR) tell a responder LSR how to send the echo reply back, using the Reply Mode field. RFC 7110 added a Reply Path TLV that can name a specific LSP for the reply.

Both tools give the initiator control, but it is getting harder for the initiator to pick a return path that is valid. If it picks badly, the reply never arrives and LSP Ping or Traceroute reports a false failure. Implementations have tried to hide this by choosing different default return paths, which do not always work and may not match what the operator wants.

This RFC does two things. It updates RFC 7110 so that the 'Reply via Specified Path' Reply Mode (value 5) can be used without a Reply Path TLV, and it adds an optional TLV that carries an ordered list of Reply Mode values.
sections.eli5: Telling a friend exactly which road to use for the answer is tricky. If you name a road that is closed, the answer gets lost. This document makes it easier to say which road, and to name backups.

sections.title: The Problem With Choosing a Return Path
sections.content:
Several things make a good default hard to compute. Some LSPs have a control channel and some do not. Some have a reverse LSP and some do not. Some have IP reachability in the reverse direction and some do not. The available return paths can also depend on whether the responder is a transit LSR or the egress LSR, and for a bidirectional LSP on whether the two directions are co-routed.

Echo requests can also end up at an unintended target with different return options, and a ping with a specific TTL or a traceroute can end at transit LSRs as well as the egress. If a responder cannot honor the return path instructions, it often drops the request. When the responder received and could verify the request but the initiator still gets no reply, the RFC calls that a false failure.

The Reply Mode 'Reply via an IPv4/IPv6 UDP packet' (value 2) works everywhere except where the responder has no IP route back to the initiator. Even so, some operators prefer the control channel or a reverse LSP when one is available.
sections.eli5: Different roads exist for different trips, and a helper partway along may not know any road home. If the helper cannot use the road you named, it just stays quiet, and you think the trip failed when it did not.

sections.title: Reply via Specified Path Without a Reply Path TLV
sections.content:
RFC 7110 required the initiator to include a Reply Path TLV with the B (Bidirectional) bit set whenever it asked for the reverse LSP, and said the TLV MUST be present for Reply Mode 5. This RFC relaxes that in two ways:

  • The 'Reply via Specified Path' Reply Mode MAY be used without a Reply Path TLV.
  • Used that way, it implies the reverse LSP. It has the same meaning as including a Reply Path TLV with the B bit set.

The text replaces the first sentence of Section 5.1 of RFC 7110: the Reply Path TLV SHOULD now be carried, and if it is absent the reply path is the reverse LSP. The reverse LSP is taken in relation to the last FEC in the Target FEC Stack TLV. The RFC limits 'reverse LSP' to reverse LSPs that can and may carry the IP-encapsulated echo reply, such as bidirectional RSVP-TE and MPLS-TP LSPs.

For compatibility, if an initiator sends mode 5 without a Reply Path TLV and gets back the return code 'Malformed echo request received', it SHOULD assume the responder does not support this mechanism.
sections.eli5: Before, to say 'come back the way I came' you had to also fill in a form. Now you can just say 'come back the way I came' and skip the form.

sections.title: The Reply Mode Order TLV
sections.content:
The new optional Reply Mode Order TLV has Type 32770. It holds one or more Reply Mode values, each one octet with no padding, in preferred order: the first is most preferred. The Length field is 2 octets and gives the length in octets of the list.

The main rules are:

  • It MUST NOT appear in an echo reply; an initiator that sees one MUST ignore it and use only the Reply Mode field.
  • It MAY appear in echo requests, but the request's Reply Mode field MUST still hold a valid value. The initiator SHOULD set it to the return path most likely to be available, in case the responder does not understand the TLV.
  • A valid TLV overrides the Reply Mode field. An invalid one is ignored as a whole.
  • It MUST contain at least one value. A value other than 5 MUST NOT repeat, and value 1 (Do not reply) MUST NOT be used.
  • Value 5 MAY repeat, but then a Reply Path TLV MUST be included for every instance of 5.

The responder SHOULD pick the first available return path and MUST put the matching Reply Mode value in its echo reply, so the initiator learns which path was used.
sections.eli5: It is a ranked list of ways to answer, best first. Your friend uses the first way that works and tells you which one they used.

sections.title: Combining the TLV With Reply Path TLVs and Proxy Ping
sections.content:
To list several specific return paths, the initiator SHOULD include several value-5 entries plus one Reply Path TLV for each path. A value 5 without a matching Reply Path TLV means the reverse LSP. If there are fewer Reply Path TLVs than consecutive 5 entries, the earlier entries get the TLVs and the later ones mean the reverse LSP. So modes {5, 5, 5} with TLVs for FEC X and FEC Y give the order FEC X, FEC Y, reverse LSP.

Two worked examples are given. To prefer the application level control channel, then FEC X, then FEC Y, then a UDP reply, the request carries modes {4, 5, 5, 2} and two Reply Path TLVs (X and Y). To prefer the reverse LSP, then a UDP reply, then FEC X, then FEC Y, it carries {5, 2, 5, 5} and three Reply Path TLVs, the first with the B bit set.

With Proxy LSP Ping (RFC 7555), a proxy LSR sending an echo request MUST copy the Reply Mode field, the Reply Mode Order TLV and the Reply Path TLVs (in order). When sending a proxy ping reply, it is RECOMMENDED that the Reply Mode Order TLV be ignored.
sections.eli5: If your list says 'road, road, road' but you only drew two special maps, the first two roads use those maps and the last one means 'the way I came.'

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4379 and RFC 7110 still apply. The new TLV gives an unauthorized source one more way to learn about a network, especially the possible return paths of an LSP. As in RFC 4379, implementations are RECOMMENDED to check the source address of echo requests against an access list. Echo messages are not encrypted, so their contents may be exposed within the MPLS domain.

For manageability, implementations are RECOMMENDED to let operators configure preferred Reply Modes. The RFC gives two example orders: for operators who care most that replies arrive, 2 then 4 then 5; for operators who want replies to test paths related to the forward LSP, 5 then 4 then 2.
sections.eli5: A ranked list also tells strangers about your roads, so only answer people you trust. Let each network owner set their favorite order.

sections.title: IANA Assignment and Scenarios
sections.content:
IANA assigned Type 32770 for the Reply Mode Order TLV in the TLVs sub-registry of the MPLS LSP Ping Parameters registry. It comes from the range 32768-49161, which is for optional TLVs that can be silently dropped if not recognized.

Appendix A shows why the TLV helps. In an incorrect forwarding case on the path A-B-C-D-E, where D wrongly switches to F, a traceroute using only mode 4 times out because F has no control channel. With the list {4, 2}, F answers with mode 2 and reports a FEC Mismatch without any timeout. In a non-co-routed bidirectional LSP, a list {5, 2} lets nodes with no reverse LSP fall back to mode 2, avoiding timeouts.
sections.eli5: The examples show a trip where one helper has no phone line. With a backup way to answer, that helper still replies, so nobody waits around.

viz.caption: REPLY MODE VALUES NAMED IN RFC 7737

items.label: Do not reply
items.desc: Must not be used in the Reply Mode Order TLV.

items.label: Reply via an IPv4/IPv6 UDP packet
items.desc: Works unless the responder has no IP route to the initiator.

items.label: Reply via application level control channel
items.desc: Uses the control channel of the LSP.

items.label: Reply via Specified Path
items.desc: Without a Reply Path TLV it means the reverse LSP.
